strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: synchronized video-to-audio generation with controllability, long-form generation, and faster sampling. These are practically meaningful pain points for current V2A systems.

The proposed system is technically plausible and combines several useful ingredients: a latent flow-matching backbone, shortcut training for few-step sampling, masked audio conditioning/outpainting, and a dedicated high-resolution audiovisual synchronization encoder.

The empirical results are promising. SALSA-V improves over FoleyCrafter and MMAudio on DeSync, FADVGG, KLPaSST, ImageBind similarity, and human-rated synchronization, while using fewer parameters than MMAudio.

The paper is generally well written, with clear motivation, architecture description, and useful implementation details in the appendix, including training schedules, batch sizes, model sizes, conditioning dropout, and VAE fine-tuning details.
The limitations section is honest about weaker subjective audio quality than MMAudio and about long-form generation being less suitable across scene cuts.
weaknesses: The central claims are stronger than the evidence. The paper claims significant state-of-the-art performance and near-real-time suitability, but the margins over MMAudio are often small, no confidence intervals or statistical tests are reported, and no actual runtime/latency measurements are provided.

The human evaluation is too small to support strong preference claims: 18 participants, 10 videos, and 180 individual scores across three systems. The paper reports MOS values but no variance, confidence intervals, participant screening details beyond 'qualified', or statistical significance.

Ablations are incomplete. Table 2 only compares model size and shortcut vs flow matching. There is no convincing ablation of the new synchronization encoder, masked training objective, audio conditioning mechanism, long-form chunking strategy, VAE fine-tuning, semantic vs synchronization features, or shortcut consistency ratio.

The long-form evaluation is not fully convincing. SALSA-V is evaluated with progressive prepending/outpainting while MMAudio is forced to process full sequences beyond its training regime; this may be a mismatched comparison. The paper also does not compare against LoVA or V-AURA in the settings most relevant to long-form generation.

The few-step generation claim is under-evaluated. Figure 5 suggests robustness at low sampling budgets, but the paper does not report wall-clock speed, hardware, real-time factor, or audio quality degradation beyond FAD/DeSync. A claim of near-real-time applications needs concrete latency evidence.

Reproducibility is limited. The manuscript does not commit to releasing code, model weights, training data, evaluation split, or generated samples; the sample URL appears blank in the extracted manuscript. Training uses a mixture of public data, filtered YouTube/Panda70M data, and a proprietary high-fidelity Foley dataset, making independent reproduction difficult.

The evaluation set is underspecified. It is described as a mixture of in-the-wild holdout videos, VGGSound test, and UnAV-100, but the number of samples, category distribution, overlap safeguards, filtering criteria, and exact split construction are not provided.

The contrastive synchronization model is a key claimed contribution, but its intrinsic evaluation is missing. The paper does not show retrieval/synchronization accuracy, offset prediction performance, comparison to Synchformer features, or evidence that the learned features directly cause the downstream gains.

The audio-conditioning analysis relies partly on a newly introduced SWSD metric and qualitative spectrograms. The metric is reasonable, but it lacks validation against perceptual judgments or baselines, and the conditioning subset is only described as 'representative' without size or selection criteria.

Ethical and data-governance issues are not adequately discussed. The work uses in-the-wild YouTube-derived data and can synthesize realistic audiovisual content, but there is no substantive discussion of licensing, consent, dataset filtering, potential misuse, watermarking/disclosure, or safeguards.

strengths: The paper targets a relevant and timely problem: synchronized, long-form video-to-audio generation with faster sampling and audio conditioning. These are useful capabilities for Foley and sound-design workflows.

The proposed system combines several reasonable technical ingredients: latent flow matching, masked in/outpainting-style conditioning, shortcut training for few-step sampling, and a dedicated audio-visual synchronization encoder. The architecture is plausible and mostly well motivated.

The evaluation attempts to cover multiple aspects of the claim, including objective audio quality metrics, semantic alignment, synchronization, few-step sampling, long-form generation, audio-conditioned outpainting, and a human listening study.

The paper is generally readable, with clear high-level motivation and enough implementation detail to understand the main training setup, model sizes, conditioning signals, optimizers, and datasets at a broad level.
weaknesses: The central claims are stronger than the evidence supports. The paper claims highly synchronized, high-fidelity, unconstrained-length, near-real-time generation, but runtime is not reported, long-form evaluation is only shown up to 60 seconds, and the long-form method is iterative chunk extension with known failure modes rather than truly unconstrained generation.

The experimental evidence is thin relative to the breadth of claims. Many key results are presented only as plots or qualitative spectrograms without exact values, confidence intervals, statistical tests, or sufficient sample-size details. Improvements over MMAudio in Table 1 are often small, e.g. DeSync 0.497 vs. 0.521 and overall MOS 3.43 vs. 3.29, while subjective audio quality is worse than MMAudio.

The ablation study is inadequate. Table 2 only compares flow matching vs. shortcut and model size. There is no convincing ablation of the learned synchronization features against Synchformer-style features, no ablation of masked training for audio conditioning or long-form generation, and no decomposition of the contributions that supposedly drive the main gains.

The human study is under-specified and small. The paper says 18 participants and 10 videos, but the stated 180 individual scores is confusing given three systems and three rating axes. It does not report variance, significance, participant screening details, presentation order controls beyond shuffling, or whether the MOS differences are meaningful.

The comparison protocol raises fairness and reproducibility concerns. The authors train on a mixture of VGGSound, Moments-in-Time, Panda70M-derived YouTube data, WavCaps, AudioSetCaps, and a high-fidelity studio Foley dataset, but baselines likely have different training data. The test set composition and filtering are not specified enough to rule out overlap or selection bias.

Reproducibility is weak. The manuscript does not provide code, model checkpoints, exact dataset lists, filtering thresholds, preprocessing scripts, or enough details to reconstruct the proprietary/in-the-wild and studio Foley training data. The line 'Samples are available at .' appears to have a missing link, which is especially problematic for an audio generation paper.

The audio-conditioning evaluation is not convincing. The SWSD metric is newly introduced and evaluated on an unspecified 'representative subset'; the metric itself involves random subsampling and projections, but no robustness analysis is given. The evidence for preserving reference spectral characteristics is therefore mostly qualitative.

The long-form evaluation is potentially biased toward the proposed method. SALSA-V uses progressive prepending/outpainting while MMAudio processes full sequences at once, and the explanation attributes MMAudio degradation to unseen positional embeddings. This may be true, but the paper does not compare against chunked or sliding-window versions of baselines, nor does it analyze accumulated errors across cuts or scene changes beyond a brief limitation.

The paper does not adequately discuss research ethics and data governance. It uses large-scale YouTube-derived data and a studio Foley dataset, but does not discuss licensing, consent, copyright, dataset filtering beyond synchronization, potential misuse for synthetic media, or watermarking/disclosure.

Presentation has several issues that reduce confidence: missing sample URL, some vague references to figures/sections, limited numerical reporting for Figure 5 and Figure 6, and claims such as 'significantly outperforms' without significance testing.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem in video-to-audio generation: synchronized, long-form, controllable, and fast Foley-style audio synthesis. The combination of masked flow matching for audio conditioning/outpainting, shortcut training for few-step sampling, and stronger audiovisual synchronization features is practically meaningful rather than merely incremental.

The empirical results are convincing overall. SALSA-V improves over FoleyCrafter and MMAudio on synchronization metrics and human-rated synchronization, with DeSync 0.497 vs 0.521 for MMAudio and human sync MOS 3.52 vs 2.92. It is also competitive or best on several objective quality/alignment metrics, including FADVGG, KLPaSST, and ImageBind similarity.

The few-step and long-form evaluations are a clear strength. Figure 5 shows that SALSA-V degrades much less than MMAudio at low sampling budgets and maintains substantially better FAD/DeSync at 60 seconds, supporting the main claims about shortcut sampling and iterative outpainting.

The paper is clearly written and technically coherent. The architecture, conditioning signals, masking setup, shortcut loss, training recipe, and VAE modifications are described in enough detail to understand the method.

The authors include useful ablations on model size and shortcut vs standard flow matching, showing that shortcut training does not noticeably harm 32-step quality. They also provide a human listening study with blind randomized trials across semantic fit, synchronization, and audio quality.
The limitations section is honest about lower subjective audio quality than MMAudio and about the fragility of progressive long-form generation across scene cuts.
weaknesses: The evaluation is strong but still leaves important gaps. The human study is small, covering 18 participants, 10 videos, and 180 scores, and the paper does not report confidence intervals, significance tests, inter-rater agreement, or per-category breakdowns. This weakens claims of subjective superiority, especially since the overall MOS margin over MMAudio is modest and SALSA-V is worse on audio quality MOS.

The long-form claim is somewhat overstated. The paper argues for unconstrained-length generation, but the quantitative evaluation appears limited to up to 60 seconds and mostly objective metrics. There is no human evaluation of long-form outputs, no stress test over many minutes, and no detailed analysis of accumulated drift or failure across scene changes beyond the limitations discussion.

Ablations are incomplete for the central components. The paper does not isolate the contribution of the new contrastive synchronization model against Synchformer-style features inside the generator, nor does it provide a direct ablation of masked training for outpainting/conditioning beyond qualitative examples and the conditioning-length analysis. This makes it hard to attribute gains cleanly.

Reproducibility is only partial. Many implementation details are provided, but there is no explicit code/model release statement, the training uses a high-fidelity studio Foley dataset that appears non-public, and the filtering thresholds for the large in-the-wild/Panda70M-derived data are described only at a high level. Reproducing the exact system would likely be difficult.

The paper claims near-real-time applicability but does not report wall-clock generation speed, hardware, latency, memory, or throughput. Few-step sampling is a useful proxy, but it does not by itself establish real-time or near-real-time deployment feasibility.

The comparison set could be broader for long-form generation. Since LoVA and V-AURA are discussed as long-form-related prior work, their absence from the main long-form quantitative comparison should be justified more explicitly.

Ethical and legal considerations are underdeveloped. The work uses in-the-wild YouTube/Panda70M-derived data and generates realistic audio for video, but the manuscript does not meaningfully discuss consent, copyright/licensing, misuse for manipulated media, or safeguards.

strengths: The paper targets an important and practically relevant problem in video-to-audio generation: synchronized, high-fidelity, long-form Foley with faster inference and audio conditioning. The combination of masked flow matching, shortcut training, and a higher-resolution synchronization feature extractor is well motivated.

The empirical results are strong across several axes. SALSA-V improves DeSync substantially over prior systems in Table 1, remains competitive or best on FAD/KL/ImageBind-style metrics, and shows much better few-step behavior than MMAudio and Frieren in Figure 4 and Table 3.

The work includes useful ablations and diagnostics: shortcut versus vanilla flow matching, parameter scaling, generation speed, sampling-step sensitivity, long-form duration curves, and audio-conditioning analyses in the appendix.

The presentation is generally clear. The method sections explain the synchronization model, masked objective, and shortcut loss sufficiently to understand the design choices, and the limitations/impact statement acknowledges long-form scene-change issues and misuse risks.

The human study, though small, evaluates perceptual fit, synchronization, and audio quality rather than relying only on proxy metrics; the synchronization gain is especially consistent with the objective results.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is a material weakness. Training uses a mixture of VGGSound, Moments-in-Time, Panda70M-derived in-the-wild video, WavCaps, AudioSetCaps, and a high-fidelity studio Foley set, but filtering thresholds, dataset composition, captions, and the proprietary Foley data are not sufficiently specified. No code/model release is described, and the listed project page is blank in the manuscript.

The central long-form claim is only partially supported. The model is trained on crops up to 15 seconds and achieves longer generation through progressive outpainting with a short prepended context; this is useful, but not the same as demonstrating robust long-horizon global coherence. The paper itself notes problems at scene cuts, yet the experiments do not systematically evaluate cuts, changing events, accumulated drift, or artifacts over substantially longer timelines.

The evaluation relies heavily on learned proxy metrics, some of which may be insensitive to perceptual artifacts or biased toward model/dataset choices. The human study covers only 10 videos and 18 participants, with no confidence intervals, statistical tests, or per-category breakdowns, making it hard to judge robustness of the subjective gains, especially for overall quality where the margins are small.

Important ablations are missing. There is no direct isolation of the proposed synchronization pretraining versus Synchformer-style features, no ablation of the masked audio objective for long-form generation, no comparison of different audio-conditioning context lengths in the main evaluation, and no analysis of whether the private/filtered data rather than the modeling changes explains part of the improvement.

Comparison fairness is somewhat unclear. Baselines differ in parameter count, training data, supported input length, and inference setup; some long-form comparisons put MMAudio outside its training length while SALSA-V uses a bespoke chunked procedure. This is a valid deployment comparison but should be separated more clearly from architectural capability.

The novelty is meaningful but mostly integrative: shortcut training and masked/inpainting objectives are adapted from prior work, and the synchronization encoder uses large pretrained backbones. The contribution is valuable for the domain, but less conceptually novel than the framing sometimes suggests.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem in video-to-audio generation: producing synchronized, high-quality audio for longer videos while reducing sampling cost. These are practically meaningful concerns for Foley, sound design, and interactive creative workflows.

The proposed system is coherent and technically plausible. Combining latent flow matching, shortcut training for few-step sampling, masked audio conditioning/outpainting, and dedicated synchronization features is a reasonable design for the stated goals.

The empirical section covers several relevant axes: standard V2A quality, synchronization, few-step generation, long-form generation, audio conditioning, efficiency, and a small human study. The reported results are often competitive or better than strong baselines such as MMAudio, LoVA, Frieren, FoleyCrafter, and AudioX.

The appendix provides useful implementation details, including optimizer settings, batch sizes, training steps, conditioning dropout, model sizes, VAE fine-tuning, and human evaluation interface details. This improves reproducibility relative to many systems papers.
The paper is generally readable, with clear motivation and a well-organized method section. The figures and tables mostly support the narrative.
weaknesses: The core contribution is more of a system-level combination than a clearly novel method. Shortcut training, masked in/outpainting, pretrained video/audio encoders, contrastive synchronization features, and latent diffusion/flow architectures are all adapted from prior work; the paper does not fully isolate which component is responsible for the gains.

The ablation evidence is insufficient. Table 2 mainly varies model size and shortcut vs. vanilla flow matching at 32 steps, but there is no strong ablation of the custom synchronization model, VideoPrism backbone, masked training objective, audio conditioning mechanism, VAE fine-tuning, conditioning dropout, or outpainting strategy. This weakens the causal support for several claims.

The evaluation may not be fully fair or reproducible. The test set is a mixed collection including holdout in-the-wild videos, VGGSound test, and UnAV-100, but its exact composition, size, selection process, and overlap controls are not sufficiently specified. Some training data are also private or weakly described, including in-the-wild YouTube videos and a studio Foley set.

Human evaluation is too small to strongly support the subjective claims. It uses 18 participants, 10 videos, and 180 scores, with no confidence intervals, significance tests, participant screening details beyond “qualified,” or analysis of inter-rater variability. The overall-quality difference over MMAudio is modest, while audio fidelity is actually lower than MMAudio in Table 1.

Several headline claims are stronger than the evidence. “Near-real-time” is asserted, but the reported 4-step generation time is 0.71s for a 10-second clip on an A100, which is promising but still hardware-dependent and not demonstrated in an interactive pipeline. Long-form generation is evaluated mostly with objective metrics and limited durations, not with robust user studies or scene-cut stress tests.

Long-form generation has a known failure mode that is central rather than incidental: progressive outpainting can carry inappropriate sound characteristics across scene changes. The limitations section acknowledges this, but the experiments do not quantify performance on videos with cuts, topic changes, silent intervals, or multiple acoustic regimes.

The audio-conditioning evaluation relies partly on a newly introduced SWSD metric and a “representative subset,” but the subset definition, size, and robustness are unclear. It is therefore hard to know whether the conditioning result generalizes beyond selected cases with repeated characteristic sounds.

Reproducibility remains limited despite some implementation details. The paper does not provide a concrete code release, exact filtered dataset lists, filtering thresholds, random seeds, evaluation sample lists, or enough detail to recreate the private training corpus. Compute requirements are also substantial and only partially characterized.

The ethical discussion is brief. It correctly notes media-manipulation risks, but does not discuss watermarking, provenance, misuse evaluation, dataset consent/licensing, or how realistic generated sounds could affect evidentiary video, surveillance, or misinformation settings.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely video-to-audio problem: synchronized, long-form, controllable, and fast Foley generation. The combination of shortcut-augmented flow matching, masked audio conditioning/outpainting, and high-resolution audiovisual synchronization features is well motivated and practically useful.

Empirical results are strong overall. SALSA-V improves over strong recent baselines on synchronization metrics, ImageBind alignment, long-form 30s evaluation against LoVA, and few-step generation against MMAudio and Frieren. The 4-step and 8-step results are especially compelling for practical deployment.

The evaluation is reasonably broad, covering objective quality/alignment metrics, few-step sampling behavior, long-form duration scaling, generation time, ablations on shortcut versus vanilla flow matching, model scaling, and a human listening study. This gives a coherent picture of where the method helps.

The methodology is clearly presented. The paper explains the roles of semantic video features, synchronization features, masked flow matching, and shortcut self-consistency, and the appendix provides useful implementation details such as training schedules, model sizes, conditioning dropout, and VAE fine-tuning.

The work has meaningful significance for creative audio workflows: fast synchronized generation and audio-conditioned outpainting address real limitations of existing video-to-audio models rather than only improving benchmark scores.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is incomplete. The model uses a mixture of public datasets, filtered Panda70M/YouTube data, and a high-fidelity studio Foley dataset, but the filtering thresholds, exact data composition, code, checkpoints, and project page are not provided in the manuscript. This will make independent replication difficult.

The ablation study does not fully isolate the major proposed components. There is no clear comparison of the new VideoPrism-based synchronization encoder against Synchformer-style features, no ablation of masked conditioning/outpainting in the main metrics, and limited analysis of how much each conditioning stream contributes.

The human study is useful but small: 18 participants, 10 videos, and 180 individual scores, with no confidence intervals or significance testing. The reported quality score is actually slightly lower than MMAudio despite better synchronization, so the subjective advantage is narrower than some of the prose suggests.

The long-form evaluation is promising but somewhat constrained. SALSA-V uses iterative extension with a 0.5-second reference section, while MMAudio processes the full sequence and may be disadvantaged by positional extrapolation outside its training regime. The paper would be stronger with more baselines adapted to chunked generation and more analysis of scene cuts or changing acoustic contexts.

The audio-conditioning evidence is partly qualitative and uses a selected subset of samples with characteristic sounds. The proposed SWSD metric is reasonable, but it is new and not validated against perception; more user-study or task-level evidence would better support claims about controllable Foley and sound design.

The limitations and ethics sections are honest but brief. The paper acknowledges carry-over failures across scene changes and potential misuse for deceptive media, but it does not propose concrete safeguards, watermarking, provenance mechanisms, or dataset/privacy handling procedures.
